Alright, the user is still complaining that RAM is being used heavily even after I killed the training run and its worker processes. The last command I ran showed the system memory status:

```
Mem:           121Gi        17Gi        92Gi       438Mi        12Gi       103Gi
```

So only 17 GiB is reported as used, which is a big drop from the previous ~45 GiB. However, the user says “Still using my RAM”, which suggests that the remaining 17 GiB is still considered excessive for their workflow, or perhaps there are still lingering processes that are holding onto memory that we haven't terminated.

I need to verify exactly which processes are currently consuming memory and how much. The simplest way is to run `free -h` again to get the high‑level numbers, but that alone won’t tell me which processes are responsible. A more detailed view can be obtained with `smem`, which reports proportional set size (PSS) per process and can give a total breakdown (`smem -t -k`). Unfortunately, I’m not sure if `smem` is installed on this system. If it isn’t, the command will fail, so I should provide a fallback that uses `ps` to list any processes using more than a threshold (say >300 MiB, which translates to >300 000 KB in the `$6` column of `ps aux`). The fallback will format the output similarly, showing PID, memory in GB, and the command name.

The user explicitly asked not to launch a background shell, so I must keep this as a single, immediate command. I’ll combine the two checks with an `||` so that if `smem` runs successfully, its output is used; otherwise, the `ps` pipeline runs. I’ll also limit the `ps` output to processes larger than 300 MiB to avoid overwhelming the user with tiny entries.

Thus, the command I’ll issue is:

```
free -h | head -2;
smem -t -k 2>/dev/null | tail -5 ||
ps aux --sort=-%mem | awk 'NR>1 && $6>300000 {printf "%s %.1fGB %s\n", $2, $6/1048576, substr($0, index($0,$11), 70)}'
```

The first part prints the memory summary, the second tries `smem` and shows the last few lines (which include the total), and the fallback `ps` line prints any remaining large processes. This should give the user a clear picture of what is still consuming RAM, allowing us to decide if further cleanup is needed.
